title: Is booking through a travel agent more expensive?
excerpt: Booking through a travel agent doesn’t automatically mean paying more. Here’s how commission, fees and holiday prices can work, what to compare in a quote, and when personal help might be worth having.
body:
## Is booking through a travel agent more expensive?

You’ve found a holiday online, checked the photographs and decided the pool looks considerably more appealing than the weather outside. Then someone suggests using a travel agent.

Fair question: does involving another person mean another cost?

**Booking through a travel agent can cost more, less or the same as booking directly.** There isn’t one pricing rule that covers every agent, supplier and holiday.

What matters is the total price, what’s included and whether the service helps you make a better decision. To compare properly, it helps to understand how the arrangements work.

## Do I charge a fee?

I don’t charge you a fee for researching or booking your holiday. If you book through me, I receive commission from the supplier as part of the booking arrangement.

So you can ask for my help without a separate planning or booking fee being added by me.

That doesn’t mean I can promise to beat every online price, or that my quote will always match booking directly. Prices and offers vary, which is why it’s worth comparing the full arrangements.

Other travel businesses may charge planning or service fees, so don’t assume every agent works the same way.

It’s also worth separating my service from the supplier’s booking conditions. If you later change or cancel your holiday, supplier charges may still apply. Not charging a fee for my help doesn’t remove those conditions.

## Why might two prices be different?

Sometimes you’re comparing different holidays without realising it.

The hotel name might match, but the cheaper option could have a different room, a different meal plan or flights at less convenient times. Baggage and transfers may also differ.

Prices can change while you’re researching, and promotions have their own eligibility conditions. An offer might apply through several booking routes, including agents, or be restricted to a particular way of booking.

There’s no reliable shortcut such as “online is always cheaper” or “agents always get special prices”.

If you’ve found a quote you like, keep the full details and note when you checked it. A screenshot showing only the hotel name and a price gives us rather a lot of detective work before there’s anything useful to compare.

## Compare the whole quote

Before deciding which option offers better value, check these details side by side:

- **Travellers and dates:** the same party, children’s ages, departure date and duration.
- **Flights:** airports, timings and any connections.
- **Accommodation:** exact room category, occupancy and meal plan.
- **Baggage:** the allowance you need, rather than simply whether “baggage” is mentioned.
- **Transfers:** whether they’re included and what type they are.
- **Total payment:** the full holiday cost and any applicable fees, not just the deposit.
- **Booking conditions:** payment deadlines and the terms for changes or cancellation.

Then consider your own priorities.

If you need separate sleeping space for the children, a cheaper room without it may not be a useful saving. If walking long distances is difficult, a hotel’s position deserves more attention than its star rating.

Equally, paying more doesn’t automatically buy a better holiday. There should be a clear reason why an option suits you.

## What does a personal consultant add?

At Planned by Jay, I personally research suitable options and help customers progress bookings through New Travel Holidays.

My starting point is understanding what you want from the holiday: who’s going, what you want to spend, what matters most and what you’d rather avoid.

That helps turn a broad search into a manageable shortlist. “Somewhere warm with a nice hotel” could lead in several directions. Add a manageable transfer, a particular room arrangement and restaurants within an easy walk, and the research becomes much more useful.

Sometimes the valuable work is spotting a question that needs answering before you book. Is that essential room feature confirmed, or merely requested? Does the transfer suit your equipment? Is the facility you want operating during your dates?

A website filter can help find possibilities. Those details may need a specific answer from the supplier.

## What are the limitations?

A personal consultant cannot guarantee the lowest price everywhere, access every supplier or make an unsuitable option suitable.

Using an agent also doesn’t remove the supplier’s booking conditions. Changes may depend on availability and involve charges. Help with an amendment isn’t a promise that the amendment will be possible or free.

Ask what support is available after booking, how to make contact and which emergency arrangements apply while you’re away. A personal service should be explained clearly; it shouldn’t be assumed to mean round-the-clock availability.

For an existing tour-operator package, the agent helps arrange a holiday put together by that operator. More specialised arrangements need the appropriate booking structure. Choosing flights and a hotel separately is not, by itself, an explanation of who is responsible for the resulting booking.

## Check protection separately from price

Don’t assume that using an agent automatically makes every travel purchase ATOL protected.

Ask what protection applies to the particular arrangements and who provides it. For an ATOL-protected booking, you should receive an ATOL Certificate when you first pay, including a deposit. Check that its details match your trip.

ATOL is financial protection, not travel insurance. It isn’t a general promise that every problem during a holiday will be covered.

## When does using an agent make sense?

If you know exactly what you want and are comfortable checking and booking it yourself, arranging it directly may suit you.

Personal help becomes particularly useful when you’re undecided, short of time or trying to make several requirements work together. You’re looking for suitable choices and clear answers, as well as a price.

I wouldn’t ask you to judge a holiday purely on the lowest figure. I wouldn’t ask you to ignore that figure either. The aim is to understand what you’re buying and feel comfortable with the decision.

If you have a holiday in mind, tell me your plans, budget and what matters most, and I’ll help you explore suitable options.
